title: Post-Deployment Safety Drift Detection on Publicly Available API Models

original_idea.title: Post-Deployment Safety Drift Detection on Publicly Available API Models
original_idea.problem: Models are updated silently after deployment, but safety evaluations are point-in-time. There is no lightweight protocol for tracking whether a model's safety behavior has drifted.
original_idea.direction: Design a small reproducible test suite of ~50 safety-sensitive prompts. Run it against the same model API endpoint at weekly intervals over the project duration. Log response hashes and refusal rates. Visualize any drift. Propose a minimal 'canary eval' standard.
original_idea.why_it_matters: Silent model updates are common. If safety properties drift, users and regulators have no way to know. A reproducible drift-detection protocol has direct policy relevance.
original_idea.relevant_context: Post-deployment safety tracking is explicitly listed as an open problem. The FLI AI Safety Index grades companies poorly on monitoring and control interventions.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: drift detection protocol enables continuous safety monitoring, which is essential for regulatory accountability. The 'canary eval' concept has independent value as a standard.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Designing 50 prompts, running them weekly via API, and logging results uses standard scripting skills. Visualization is basic. Fully accessible to beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: The experimental design is simple but requires longitudinal data collection over weeks, which is constrained by the project timeline rather than effort. Within 30 hours of work the design and first few runs are achievable but full drift measurement needs time.

novelty.reasoning: The problem of silent model updates and safety drift is well-documented: GPT-4o behavioral changes were reported without notice in Feb 2025, and tools like Confident AI, Langfuse, Arize AI exist for LLM monitoring. However, most existing work focuses on general behavioral drift (response length, semantic similarity) rather than safety-specific drift with a reproducible test suite. The proposed 'canary eval' concept -- a minimal standardized safety-specific drift detection protocol -- is a distinct contribution. The longitudinal design with response hashes and refusal rate tracking specifically for safety prompts has not been formalized as a standard, though the individual components exist.
